content_metadata.description: A video explaining the concept of velocity addition in the context of special relativity, using animations, equations, and thought experiments.

What speed is the train traveling at in the second animation?

trimmingSuggestions.description: The initial black screen and simple title card could be shortened to quickly introduce the topic.
The walking animation could be sped up to make it more dynamic.
Consider combining Scenes 2 and 3 and using a faster animation for both the walking and kicking actions to streamline the explanation of velocity addition in different scenarios.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Now that we have a feel for the effects of special relativity, let's look at how fast
things can go in this relativistic world.
You'll recall from our previous segment on the speed of light, the classical transformation
simply added the speed of movement in a reference frame to the speed of the reference frame itself.
Here we see the person walking on the moving train.
We simply added his walking speed to the train's speed to get the speed seen by an observer
on the ground.
In special relativity, the clock on the train is running a bit slower, and the distance
the person walked is a little bit shorter as seen by the observer on the ground.
So this calculation of the total velocity is a bit less than the Galilean calculation,
but at these speeds it is too small a difference to notice.
Now let's shift the super train into high gear and say his velocity is 8 tenths of the speed
of light.
And the person on the train kicks the ball at one half the speed of light.
If the Galilean transformations were correct, the person on the ground would add these
together and see the ball traveling faster than the speed of light.
But to keep the speed of light a constant, the new relativistic equations tell us the
person on the ground would see the ball traveling a lot slower than that at 9 tenths of speed
of light.
You can even see that with the relativistic equations if the train was traveling at
point 8 times the speed of light, and a light was turned on, the person on the ground
will see the light traveling at the speed of light, just like the person on the train
will.
In the most extreme case, suppose we had two photons traveling towards each other.
Here's the northern hemisphere's summer triangle, the Vega, Altair, and Deneb.
Let's say one photon is traveling from Deneb to Altair and the other one is traveling
from Altair to Deneb.
Of course each of them is traveling at the speed of light, so we would see their closing
speed at two times the speed of light.
And if we look at it from the point of view of one of the photons, we see that it sees
them closing at the speed of light, not twice the speed of light.
